analysis.one_liner: Extends the federal nuclear-accident liability and insurance system for power plant operators, including new modular reactors.
analysis.headline: The Senate committee approved the bill with an amendment in July 2005, but it sat on the Senate calendar and never got a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would reauthorize the Price-Anderson system, which requires nuclear plant operators to carry liability insurance and pools industry money to pay victims of a nuclear accident, while capping the total amount operators can be made to pay. It would extend the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's authority to indemnify certain licensees through 2025, extend annual reports to Congress on the system, raise the maximum deferred premiums licensees can be charged after an incident, and treat clusters of small modular reactors at one site as a single large facility under the system.
analysis.who_benefits: Nuclear plant operators and licensees gain the most: the federal framework that limits their liability for a catastrophic nuclear incident and backstops their insurance obligations continues instead of lapsing. Private nuclear insurers keep the mandated market for their policies. Developers of small modular reactors gain a clear path into the system, since a group of small reactors at one site would count as one large facility subject to (and protected by) the liability framework.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nuclear plant operators and modular reactor developers

how_it_helps.text: Extends NRC authority to indemnify certain licensees, and the overall Price-Anderson indemnification guidelines, through December 31, 2025, instead of letting them lapse at the end of 2003.

Raises the maximum standard deferred premium that can be charged to a licensee after a nuclear incident from $63 million to $95.8 million (inflation-adjusted), and the annual maximum from $10 million to $15 million, so industry contributions to the compensation pool grow modestly.

Directs the NRC to treat a combination of small reactors (each between 100,000 and 300,000 electrical kilowatts, at a single site, combined capacity up to 1.3 million kilowatts) as a single facility of 100,000 kilowatts or more for financial-protection purposes, bringing modular reactor projects into the liability framework.
Extends the requirement that the NRC and Energy Secretary report to Congress on whether to continue or modify the Price-Anderson Act.

analysis.who_pays: Potential victims of a catastrophic nuclear accident bear the tail risk: the bill works through 'limitation of liability arising from nuclear incidents in excess of the level of financial protection required of the licensee,' so damages beyond what the required insurance and industry pool cover are capped rather than fully recoverable from operators. The federal government also remains on the hook for the incidents it indemnifies.

drawbacks.text: The core of the Price-Anderson regime is a cap: liability for a nuclear incident is limited in excess of the financial protection the licensee is required to carry, so victims of an accident larger than the insurance pool cannot collect full damages from the plant owner.

Deferred premiums charged to licensees after an incident are payable over time and capped ($95.8 million total, $15 million per year under the bill), so the industry's maximum contribution after a disaster is bounded even if actual losses are far larger.
Extending the framework for more than two decades locks in a liability regime whose adequacy Congress would only review through annual reports, not a fresh up-or-down decision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The system has a real public benefit: it guarantees a funded, no-fault compensation channel for nuclear accident victims, paid into by the industry rather than nothing at all. But its defining feature is the liability cap, which shifts the worst-case, low-probability, catastrophic-loss risk away from plant operators and onto potential victims and the public. The bill modestly raises what industry can be charged after an incident while extending the capped-liability framework for over twenty years, so the balance tilts toward the industry it regulates.

outcome.mechanism: The Environment and Public Works Committee approved it with an amendment and it was placed on the Senate calendar in July 2005, but Senate leaders never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 20, 2005 by Senator Voinovich and read twice and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee.
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on June 8, 2005, and it was reported on July 1, 2005 with Senate Report 109-99.
The reported bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 153) on July 1, 2005, and no further floor action ever occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nuclear plant operators were not left in limbo by this bill's death: Congress reauthorized the same Price-Anderson provisions later in 2005 through the Energy Policy Act of 2005, so the industry ended the Congress with the extended liability framework this bill would have provided. No one lost anything of substance from this particular bill dying.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nuclear plant operators, reauthorized later anyway

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls were ever taken on the bill; the sponsor and committee chairman were Republicans and one of its two cosponsors was a Democrat.

industries.industry: Nuclear power plant operators and licensees
industries.note: The bill extends the liability framework that caps what operators must pay after a catastrophic nuclear incident, while modestly raising the deferred premiums they can be charged ($95.8 million total, $15 million a year). The cap is the industry's core benefit: worst-case losses beyond required insurance are not fully recoverable from plant owners.

The Price-Anderson system requires operators to carry private primary insurance and feed an industry-wide pool, so the extension preserves a federally mandated customer base for nuclear insurers. Victims get a funded compensation channel, but one bounded by the liability cap.

The bill lets a cluster of small reactors at one site count as a single facility of 100,000 kilowatts or more for financial-protection purposes, giving next-generation reactor projects a defined way into the liability and insurance system.
